LADDER LOGIC LANGUAGE
Ladder logic diagrams illustrate operations. S2 MOTOR 101 102 MOTOR S3 S4 LAMP 103 104 LAMP Operational Ladder Logic Diagram Diagram
DISCUSSION
The input statements may be arranged to describe OR and AND logic conditions. 111 MOTOR 112 Ladder Logic OR Logic AND Logic
AND logic is used when the combined conditions of two or more inputs determine the output. The motor starts only when inputs 101 and 102 are true. 01 102 MOTOR OR Logic AND Logic
Both inputs 101 and 102 must be true for output execution. The motor will not start if only one of the inputs is true.
OR logic is used when the condition of any one of the inputs can determine the output. The motor starts when inputs 111 or 112 are true.
AND and OR logic conditions may be nested together. Output 009 is true when both inputs 101 and 102 are true or when 103 is true.
The maximum number and acceptable arrangements of the inputs depends on the particular type of PLC used.

INPUT INSTRUCTIONS
We are familiar with the normally open and normally closed types of input instructions. These are identified as relay logic instructions because they operate using a single bit of data.
NORMALLY OPENED - A normally opened contact is true (closed) when the applied condition is 1 (ON), and false (opened) when the applied condition is 0 (OFF). Also called Examine if Closed (XIC).

NORMALLY CLOSED - A normally closed contact is false (opened) when the applied condition is 1 (ON), and true (closed) when the applied condition is 0 (OFF). The comparison input instructions are used to compare data values. The actual symbol used and the information needed may vary depending on the programming system used.
For example, the less than comparison instruction determines if the value from source A is less than the value from source B.
The input is true as long as the value from source A is less than the value from source B.
Comparison input instructions are easily applied to industrial processes such as using the input to control a conveyor belt.
The PLC programmer can use a less than or equal to instruction to determine if a certain number of items have passed by a sensor.
The input instruction is true and the conveyor belt continues to turn as long as the count (source B) is less than or equal to the set value (source A).
The conveyor belt stops as soon as the sensor indicates that the count exceeds the set number.

The next part of the experiment demonstrates how a sequencer instruction may be used to control traffic lights.
One set of traffic lights controls traffic traveling east and west.
The other set controls traffic traveling north and south. This set also has an additional turn signal.
Each light is given a number to correspond to a PLC trainer's LED. When the LED is illuminated, the traffic light is illuminated.
The program starts with all of the LED's off.
Pressing the start button once displays the contents of position 1 in the data file. LED's 2 and 3 illuminate indicating that traffic lights 2 and 3 are lit.
The east-west traffic has a green light and the north-south traffic has a red light.

Pressing the start button a second time displays the contents of position 2 in the data file. LED's 3 and 1 illuminate so east-west traffic has a yellow light while north-south traffic still has the red light....

Pressing the start button a third time displays the contents of position 3 in the data file. LED's 6 and 0 illuminate so east-west traffic now has a red light and north-south traffic has the turn signal...
Each time the start button is pressed the contents of a different position in the data file are displayed. The LED's change accordingly indicating that the traffic lights also change.
The cycle starts over at position 1 after position 6 is reached.
